initial.source: # Write the full assignment here. The practice example has its own editor.

solution:
if test "$#" -ne 1; then
    printf 'Usage: labels SOURCE\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
source=$1
if test -f "$source"; then :; else
    printf 'Usage: labels SOURCE\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
number=0
while IFS= read -r line || test -n "$line"; do
    number=$((number + 1))
    printf '%s: [%s]\n' "$number" "$line"
done < "$source"

teaching.try_change: Remove only IFS= in the practice script, Run, and compare the spaces around Gate open. Restore it, then remove the || test -n part and see the final last record disappear.

concepts.title: Whitespace can be part of the label
concepts.text: Ordinary read -r line trims spaces and tabs at the edges. IFS= read -r line temporarily asks that one read to keep them; it does not change later splitting. -r keeps backslashes as text. Type the script in the editor and use Run against the sample inputs; no real file or shell is involved.

concepts.title: A newline and the end of input differ
concepts.text: read consumes the newline and returns status 0 for a complete line, even a blank line. At the end it returns 1. A final nonempty line without a newline is still assigned to line, despite status 1. The condition read ... || test -n "$line" handles that last record; empty EOF stops it.

concepts.title: Keep data out of the format
concepts.text: Use a fixed printf format and quoted values, such as printf '%s: [%s]\n' "$number" "$line". Percent signs inside the label then stay data. The script creates source, number and line; the lab supplies the filename as $1, not a pre-created line variable.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on Number a handover queue and Keep the final record when input ends. Revisit them for numbering, read loops and final partial records; this introduction adds preserving edge whitespace.

scenarios.explanation: A successful loop preserves the line as data, numbers even empty records, and keeps a nonempty final partial line. The literal-empty IFS prefix changes only that read; quoted printf values prevent spaces, backslashes and percent signs becoming commands or formatting. Validation happens before any file change.

scenarios.title: Do not publish a pipeline that failed
scenarios.summary: Distinguish no matches from a failed producer before replacing a report.
scenarios.objective: Take exactly one SOURCE filename. Supplied source filenames are distinct from errors.txt and keep.txt. Select every line containing literal uppercase ERROR, sort whole lines in C-byte order and remove duplicates. On a valid source, replace errors.txt with those records (one newline each), print Report updated and a newline, return 0 and preserve every other file. No matches or an empty source are valid: publish an empty report. On a missing source, leave every file unchanged, return 2 and send the grep missing-file diagnostic followed by Report unavailable and a newline to standard error; stdout stays empty. Bad argument count: only Usage: errors SOURCE and a newline on standard error, status 2, no changes. Filenames are supplied flat basenames.

cases.name: Missing producer input
cases.stderr:
grep: missing.log: No such file or directory
Report unavailable

files./work/events.log:

	ERROR tab	
ERROR 100%
 ERROR pad

after./work/events.log:

solution:
if test "$#" -ne 1; then
    printf 'Usage: errors SOURCE\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
set -o pipefail
matches=$(grep -F ERROR "$1" | sort | uniq)
status=$?
if test "$status" -gt 1; then
    printf 'Report unavailable\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if test -n "$matches"; then
    printf '%s\n' "$matches" > errors.txt
else
    printf '' > errors.txt
fi
printf 'Report updated\n'

concepts.title: The last stage can hide an earlier failure
concepts.text: By default, a pipeline reports only its last stage status. grep may fail to open the source, while sort and uniq still accept empty input and succeed. Explicit set -o pipefail changes the pipeline result to the rightmost failing stage, or 0 when all succeed. Each new Run starts with this option off.

concepts.title: No matching lines is a useful result
concepts.text: For the supported grep -F form, 0 means matches, 1 means no matches, and 2 means a file error. No matches is not a broken source. Save status=$? immediately after the pipeline or capture before another command replaces it. The simulator still reports unsupported syntax and resource limits as ungraded errors.

concepts.title: Build the candidate before writing
concepts.text: matches=$(...) captures output and inherits pipefail. It strips trailing newlines, so put back one with printf when matches is nonempty; use an empty printf for no matches. Validate status before > errors.txt, because > empties an old file immediately. The script creates matches and status; $1 comes from the lab. Checking the producer separately is also a valid approach.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on Keep every label while reading text, Investigate findings without losing their status and Count locations without losing repeats. Revisit them for literal records, saved status, captures, sorting and deduplication; this introduction adds pipeline failure handling.

scenarios.explanation: The report is a candidate until its producer status is known. pipefail exposes a failing grep that successful sort/uniq would hide; checking grep separately is equivalent. No matches produces an empty valid report, while a file error leaves the previous report intact. Capture removes trailing newlines, so publication restores one only for nonempty data.

scenarios.title: Publish a validated text handover
scenarios.summary: Combine input validation, literal line handling and a report built before publication.
scenarios.objective: Write report SOURCE OUTPUT. Require exactly two nonempty flat basenames (no slash, . or ..), an existing SOURCE, and OUTPUT different from SOURCE and keep.txt. Read every source record without trimming text; handle blank lines and a final partial record. Write Entry: <TEXT> and a newline for each record, then Total: N and a newline to OUTPUT. An empty source produces only Total: 0 and a newline. Success: print Published report and a newline, status 0, no error output. Preserve SOURCE, keep.txt and every other file. On any invalid count, name, missing source or protected output, print only Usage: report SOURCE OUTPUT and a newline to standard error, status 2, and change no file. All work is simulated; this is not an atomic or concurrent filesystem transaction.

initial.source: # Write the full assignment here. The practice example has its own editor.

cases.name: Empty input still has a total

after./work/report.txt:
Entry: <>
Entry: <Café>
Entry: < 展示 >
Total: 3

solution:
usage() {
    printf 'Usage: report SOURCE OUTPUT\n' >&2
    exit 2
}
if test "$#" -ne 2; then usage; fi
source=$1
destination=$2
case "$source" in
    ''|*/*|.|..) usage ;;
esac
case "$destination" in
    ''|*/*|.|..|keep.txt) usage ;;
esac
if test "$source" = "$destination"; then usage; fi
if test -f "$source"; then :; else usage; fi
report=$(count=0
    while IFS= read -r line || test -n "$line"; do
        printf 'Entry: <%s>\n' "$line"
        count=$((count + 1))
    done < "$source"
    printf 'Total: %s\n' "$count"
)
printf '%s\n' "$report" > "$destination"
printf 'Published report\n'

teaching.example:
usage() {
    printf 'Usage: practice SOURCE OUTPUT\n' >&2
    exit 2
}
if test "$#" -ne 2; then usage; fi
source=$1
destination=$2
case "$source" in
    ''|*/*|.|..) usage ;;
esac
case "$destination" in
    ''|*/*|.|..|keep.txt) usage ;;
esac
if test "$source" = "$destination"; then usage; fi
if test -f "$source"; then :; else usage; fi
report=$(count=0
    while IFS= read -r line || test -n "$line"; do
        printf 'Notice: <%s>\n' "$line"
        count=$((count + 1))
    done < "$source"
    printf 'Notices: %s\n' "$count"
)
printf '%s\n' "$report" > "$destination"
printf 'Example published\n'
teaching.inputs: The practice example supplies its own arguments and virtual files. It publishes Notice: <TEXT> rows and Notices: N to handover.txt, then prints Example published. The assignment has its own Entry/Total/Published report interface. The script creates its own variables; drafts remain separate.
teaching.try_change: In the separate example, change only the final output destination to keep.txt. Observe why validation must use the same destination that publication uses. Restore it, then remove IFS= and compare the spaces in Front desk.

concepts.title: Validate before opening the output
concepts.text: The > operator can erase an existing file before a later error is noticed. Check all arguments and preservation rules first. A case pattern such as */* detects a slash; quoted empty text, . and .. are invalid names for this task. No real directory or host file exists here.

concepts.title: Build one candidate in a capture
concepts.text: A capture can run the entire read loop and print its total. Variables changed inside it stay there, so compute and print the count inside the capture as well. Quoted "$report" preserves spaces and embedded line breaks. All capture text shares the existing memory, output and instruction limits.

concepts.title: Publish only after the candidate is ready
concepts.text: The final count line (Notices in this example, Total in the assignment) ensures the candidate is nonempty even for an empty source. Capture removes its final newline; printf '%s\n' "$report" restores exactly one. Only then redirect to the validated output. This protects these supplied files from validation errors; it is not a promise of crash-safe real filesystem replacement.

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on Do not publish a pipeline that failed, Preview or publish a validated release plan and Protect the report heading. Revisit them for producer checks, argument validation, case patterns and local scope; this introduction combines validation with literal line handling before publication.

scenarios.explanation: Count, path and collision validation happens first. The capture builds all entries and the total with literal line handling; its own count stays inside that scope. Only a complete candidate is written to the approved destination. Full file-map grading also verifies input, evidence and unrelated files; this is bounded simulated publication, not a crash-safe real filesystem transaction.
